wine.name: Graffigna Centenario Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, by a review of the 2007 vintage and the listings of later ones.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Tulum Valley, the warm, dry valley floor around the city of San Juan, by the listings read; no single vineyard is named for it.
wine.making: By retailers' notes of several vintages and a review of the 2007, about half of the wine was aged in oak barrels for around twelve months while the other half stayed out of wood, and the two were blended before bottling, so the oak frames the fruit rather than leading it.
wine.glass: Ripe plum and black cherry with a toasty, vanilla edge from the oak aged half, soft, rounded tannin and gentle acidity: the warm, generous manner of the Tulum Valley rather than a taut mountain Malbec.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first few years, while the fruit is fresh; it was never a wine for long keeping.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The reserve range of the house's San Juan years, printed Centenario Reserve on some vintages.
The province of origin, north of Mendoza, where the house keeps its old cellar at Desamparados.
The single grape of the wine, grown on the Tulum Valley floor.

records.table: Graffigna is the old name of San Juan wine, dated by the house to 1870, and its Centenario Malbec was the reserve red that carried it abroad: Tulum Valley Malbec, half of it aged in oak, ripe and soft, to pour young.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1870, when, by its own history, the first vineyard under the Graffigna name was planted in San Juan; other accounts give 1869 for an uncle's purchase of land at Desamparados, or 1876 for the start of the founder's own cellar. The founder came from Italy as a boy, and by the house's account he pushed the railway on to reach new drinkers in 1885 and was among the first in Argentina to sell wine under a brand. He died in 1923, on a journey to see his family in Italy. The cellar at Desamparados, with a museum named for him, became a stop for visitors to the province. The Centenario range gave the old name a reserve tier in its export years: its Malbec, from the Tulum Valley, was bottled under San Juan in the vintages of the 2000s and early 2010s. Late in 2018 Pernod Ricard Argentina agreed to sell Graffigna, with its San Juan cellar and vineyards and a vineyard at La Consulta in the Uco Valley, to the Chilean VSPT Wine Group, and the sale closed in 2019. In 2022, by a trade report, the house moved its winemaking to the Uco Valley in Mendoza. The Centenario is the taste of the San Juan Graffigna that came before that move.

wine.name: Finca Las Moras Gran Syrah
wine.sites: A blend of three San Juan valleys, by the house's page: the warm Tulum Valley at about 650 metres, the Zonda Valley at about 800 metres and the cool, high Pedernal Valley at about 1,300 metres; the share of each moves with the vintage.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel, by a retailer's note, then aged for eighteen months in new French and American oak barrels, by the house's own page, before the lots of the three valleys are blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and black pepper wrapped in the vanilla and toast of new barrels, warm and full in the San Juan manner, with ripe, rounded tannin and a fresher finish from the Pedernal share.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps for some years as the oak settles into the fruit.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's oak aged Syrah, blended from its three valleys.
The province of origin, north of Mendoza; the fruit comes from three of its valleys.
The single grape of the wine, the variety San Juan is known for.

records.table: Finca Las Moras puts three San Juan valleys into one bottle with its Gran Syrah: warm Tulum, Zonda and cool, high Pedernal Syrah, aged a year and a half in new French and American oak. Pour it with grilled meat, after an hour in a decanter.
records.story: San Juan grew vines long before 1993, mostly for everyday wine, table grapes and concentrate. Finca Las Moras dates itself to that year, when its Tulum Valley vineyards were restructured under the guidance of an Australian viticulturist, by two guides to the province's wineries. The work turned the house towards wines of quality at a time when the province was known for volume, and the guides count it among the pioneers of that turn. Syrah became its grape. The warm Tulum floor gave ripeness, and the house farmed in two valleys to the west as well: Zonda, at the foot of the Andean foothills, and Pedernal, high in the south, which its own pages call the coolest valley of the province. The Gran Syrah gathers all three, each valley at its own height, and spends eighteen months in new oak. Its 2011 vintage was reviewed by Decanter under San Juan, and in 2014 the same magazine's coverage of Argentina profiled the house as one shaking the status quo of a province long seen as a bulk region. Beside a Mendoza Malbec, the Gran Syrah shows the grape San Juan made its name with, and its warmth.

wine.name: Callia Magna Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, printed as Shiraz on some export labels.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyards in the Tulum Valley at Caucete, on poor alluvial soils of sandy loam to clay loam with little organic matter, by its 2018 sheet, between the Pie de Palo range and the Cerro Chico of Zonda.
wine.making: By the house's sheet for the 2018 vintage, half of the wine was aged for nine months in barrels, split evenly between French and American oak, and the other half kept out of wood, before the two were blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Fig and cassis with a vanilla note from the barrels, by the house's own sheet; ripe and sweet on entry, with clove, cinnamon and raspberry noted by a panel of reviewers, and soft, rounded tannin.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk within its first few years, while its ripe fruit leads; a few years more soften the oak.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: One of the house's premium ranges, made in Syrah and in Malbec.
The valley round the city of San Juan where the house's vineyards and cellar lie.
The name some export labels give the same grape, Syrah.

records.table: Callia was built for Syrah: a Tulum Valley cellar at Caucete founded in 2002 by the family behind Bodegas Salentein. Its Magna Syrah, half of it aged nine months in French and American oak, shows fig and cassis, the warm San Juan style.
records.story: Bodegas Callia was founded in 2002 by the Dutch family behind Bodegas Salentein of the Uco Valley, in the Tulum Valley at Caucete, east of the city of San Juan. The aim, in the house's own press kit, was to make the leading wines of San Juan and of Argentine Shiraz, and Syrah, the grape the province had made its name with, became its signature. Its vineyards lie on poor alluvial soils in a valley of very little rain, framed by the Pie de Palo range to the north and the Cerro Chico of Zonda, and the press kit of 2014 also counts a large estate in the high Pedernal Valley to the south. The range runs from the everyday Alta and Bella bottlings to the Magna wines and the Grand Callia blend, and the house has bottled a Criolla too. The Magna Syrah keeps to Tulum fruit, with half the wine in oak, so it shows the warm valley floor rather than the mountains. The same family's Pyros wines come from the Pedernal Valley. By its sheet for the 2018 vintage, the Magna Syrah spent nine months in barrels split between French and American oak. Taste it beside a Pyros Malbec to hear the province's two climates, the valley floor and the heights.

wine.name: Pyros Single Vineyard Block No. 4 Malbec
wine.sites: Block No. 4 of the house's vineyard on the west slope of the Pedernal hill at about 1,400 metres, the highest part of the valley by the house's pages, on very stony soils of limestone and flint, with granite and schist.
wine.making: Aged for about twelve months in French oak barrels, only about a tenth of them new in the 2018 vintage by a review's note, and given a further year in bottle before release by the importer's page; the details move with the vintage.
wine.glass: Mint, liquorice and black tea with much perfume and wild herbs over blackberry, a chalky, stony grip and fresh acidity: a lifted mountain Malbec rather than a plush one, by a critic's note.
wine.ageing: Built to keep: a critic gave one vintage a drinking window of about a decade from release, and it opens slowly in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The single parcel of the estate whose fruit makes the wine.
The high valley in the south of San Juan, named for its flint.
Greek for fire, for the sparks the valley's flints throw, by local legend.

records.table: Pyros takes its Greek name for fire from the flints of the Pedernal Valley, and its Block No. 4 Malbec comes from one stony parcel at about 1,400 metres: perfumed, minty and fresh, a mountain answer to warm San Juan. Give it an hour in a decanter.
records.story: Pedernal is Spanish for flint, and the valley that bears the name lies high in the south of San Juan, the coolest of the province's valleys by a neighbouring house's account. In 2008 the Dutch founder of Bodegas Salentein began Pyros there, with a vineyard on the west slope of the Pedernal hill at about 1,400 metres, the highest part of the valley; the vines were planted that year, by the house's sheets. The name, as the house tells it, comes from a local legend: struck together, the flints of the valley throw sparks, and the old people of the region lit their fires with them. Pyros is Greek for fire. The soils are stony, rich in limestone and flint with granite and schist, and the house mapped them closely and farmed the vineyard parcel by parcel. The Appellation Malbec gathers the estate; Block No. 4 is one parcel bottled alone, the house's case for what altitude does to San Juan Malbec. By the 2018 vintage its barrels were mostly old, a tenth of them new, so the site leads rather than the oak. The same family's Callia cellar lies in the warm Tulum Valley below, and the two together show the province's floor and its heights.

wine.name: Cara Sur Criolla Chica
wine.grapes: Criolla Chica, the grape Chile calls País and the Canaries Listán Prieto, brought to the Americas by the Spanish.
wine.sites: Old vines trained on pergolas around Barreal in the Calingasta Valley, in Paraje Hilario and other parcels at the foot of the Andes, some eighty years old by the importer's account.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts on its skins in concrete, as whole bunches in some vintages and mostly destemmed in others, then aged in concrete for some months, seven in one vintage by a critic's guide, before bottling.
wine.glass: Strawberry, red cherry and rose petal with cracked white pepper and a saline edge, pale cherry in colour, light in body, with gentle tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, within a few years of the vintage, while its red fruit is bright.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, lightly chilled; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The old mission grape of the Spanish, known in Chile as País.
Spanish for south face, after the harder southern face of Cerro Mercedario above Barreal.
A named place near Barreal in the Calingasta Valley, printed on some vintages.

records.table: Cara Sur, a tiny cellar at Barreal under the Andes, bottles Criolla Chica, the grape the Spanish brought, from old pergola vines of the Calingasta Valley. Pale, light and peppery, with strawberry and rose, it wants pouring a little cool.
records.story: Barreal lies in the Calingasta Valley, high on the Andean side of San Juan, where smallholders kept old pergolas of Criolla grapes long after most of Argentina had turned to Malbec. Two couples began Cara Sur there. By one partner's telling they first made Criollas at university in 2008, then in a parents' garage in 2011, the year the project was formed. One partner is of the family behind Familia Zuccardi in Mendoza, but Cara Sur is a project of its own. The name means south face, for the harder southern route up Cerro Mercedario, a high Andean peak seen from Barreal. The tiny cellar stands beside two of the partners' homes, takes fruit from old vines of the valley, ferments with native yeasts in concrete and adds little else. Criolla Chica is the mission grape of the Spanish, País in Chile, and little of it is left in Argentina. Until 2024 the National Wine Institute counted it a pink grape, so a red of it stood outside the list of quality wines; the partners pressed for change, and the institute's decree of 16 August 2024 raised Criolla Chica to a quality red grape. The bottle shows that old grape at altitude: light, fresh and its own.
